en: The Sūtra on the Buddha Ascending to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Preach the Dharma for His Mother, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, beneath the Pārijāta tree.
Because he pitied his mother and sought to deliver her from suffering,

Śuklodana spent the three months of the summer retreat together with a great assembly of bhikṣus— eight thousand in all, each an arhat whose outflows were exhausted, who had attained great supernormal powers and infinite majesty;
who had completely severed birth and death, were free from further defilement, had cast off the heavy burden, accomplished what was to be done, and realized their own benefit.

His mind immediately attained the patience of equanimity through his realization; having achieved liberation of mind, he was perfected in wisdom. He was a universal true sage, bringing great benefit and peace to the world as a field of merit—except for one person, the worthy Ānanda.

There were seventy-two thousand bodhisattvas, all of whom were great sages who had mastered supernatural powers, attained dhāraṇīs, and possessed unimpeded eloquence; they had each come from various other buddha-worlds to assemble together.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a retinue of countless hundreds of thousands of followers as he preached the sutra.
At that moment, there were two devaputras in the assembly named Candrarāja and Candrottarā.
The Cakravartin King of the Yuezhi immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms, knelt with one knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to inquire of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; if you would grant me leave, I shall venture to speak."
The Buddha addressed the devaputra:
“What is the meaning you wish to ask of the Tathāgata?
The Devaputra Candraprabha replied in verse:
"Regarding the multitudes of sentient beings, he gives rise to a heart of compassion;
seeking the path of the Buddha, his will is set upon the stainless nectar of immortality.
He reflects upon the conduct of his own body and extends loving-kindness and pity to all the people."
For these reasons, I have questioned the Lion of the Śākyas.
Having accumulated practice over billions of eons, he was able to endure all hardships;
he gave everything in alms, his mind tranquil and free from thought.
With an impartial mind toward all living beings, you have brought healing and transformation with perfect equanimity;
I ask this supreme truth of you who guides and benefits the masses.
If one perceives the true path, one will be naturally adorned with sublime marks.
The thirty-two marks, stainless, are the field of merit for the most eminent;
those who attain such merit pay reverence as if to a vast ocean.
Now I question the Great Sage, desiring to understand this meaning and find its ultimate rest.
If one possesses no divergent mind, then there will be no other thoughts;
always aspiring to seek sublime wisdom, one becomes a towering and honored being among men,
harboring no intent for the state of a śrāvaka and having no longing for the affairs of a pratyekabuddha.
Now I ask this question of you, who are steadfast and faultless:
whether there is profit or loss, remain equanimous toward blame and praise;
whether there is fame or notoriety, do not be moved by suffering or pleasure.
Though dwelling amidst worldly dharmas, you are not moved or shaken;
now I ask about this meaning, O one who has distanced yourself from fear.
Regarding the matter of cherishing your own body, you regard all common folk with equal mindfulness.
There has never been such variety; all are transformed within the three realms.
By cultivating a heart of loving-kindness, one is free from flattery and free from loathing.
Now I ask about this meaning: how does the Worthy One maintain the land?
With a mind constantly practicing diligence, through generosity and precepts one leaves behind evil;
his body attains tranquility, and the category of precepts is never extinguished.
Body, speech, and mind are always upright; he guides, follows, and protects [others] with compliance.
Now I ask about the supreme meaning: dwelling amidst defilement yet free from dust;
patient and gentle, having attained realization, one further pursues cultivation;
able to endure hardships and afflictions amidst crowds of agitation and negligence.
Wandering to save all beings, yet never giving rise to anger;
for this reason I ask about the meaning, desiring to resolve all doubts.
May each always exert themselves with diligence, being respectful and compliant, not deviating from the truth.
Compassionately pitying the world, he does not practice giving for his own sake;
in practicing the Way, he is never weary or satisfied, like the ocean receiving all streams.
Therefore, I ask the Most Victorious One, whose virtue is like the great ocean.
Though abiding in these three places, he does not regress from various perceptions;
with the wisdom of the noble ones, he subdues and eliminates all defilements.
Sustaining the wondrous penetration of meditative concentration, he delights in the supernormal powers.
I now ask about this meaning, so as to go everywhere and transform the multitudes.
With wisdom you have crossed to the other shore; your noble realization is boundless.
You have cast off all discursive thoughts and left the household life to uproot the very source of affliction.
Attaining mastery through serene fearlessness, And clearly understanding this wisdom of the Dharma,
I now venture to inquire of you, The Great Sage of Infinite Excellence.
Regarding the supernormal powers you have distinguished, Please explain the practice that accords with them.
Wandering through billions of buddha-fields, yet having no notion of "fields";
making offerings to billions of buddhas, yet having no notion of "buddhas"—
it is for this reason that I ask about this meaning, so that all who behold it may receive universal joy.
Having departed from the dust of desire and the māra, suddenly transforming the māra of the aggregates (skandha-māra),
abandoning the māra of death, subduing all celestial māras,
and eliminating every kind of māra, one then attains the Way of the Buddha.
Therefore, by inquiring into this meaning, one forever casts off all darkness.
It causes heaven and earth to tremble, as well as the trees and mountain crags.
Awakening to and realizing the Buddha-way, one attains immeasurable and most supreme wisdom.
If one has already attained single-mindedness and practiced the illumination of tranquil concentration,
for this reason one asks about this meaning and inquires with such a request.
You who have fully awakened to all wisdom, whose majestic radiance is most sublime—
Established in the Buddha’s teaching, you have skillfully established the practice of the Dharma;
you guide and benefit the multitude of sages, leaving none untransformed.
Now, therefore, I ask about this meaning, for you who ferry across those wandering through the three realms.
The Devaputra Candraprabha again asked the World-Honored One:
"Indeed, Great Sage!
What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining the extraordinary practices of the great sage’s supernormal powers and crossing over to the other shore?"
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s arrival at inconceivable skillful means (upāyakauśalya) and being fully equipped with the wisdom of encouragement and assistance?

What is meant by a bodhisattva regarding all dharmas as a single principle, entering into the single flavor where the destination is uniform and equal, and entering into the discourse of the equality of the single wisdom?

"What is meant by a bodhisattva reverently upholding profound precepts and practicing without negligence, thereby attaining the unsurpassed, true, and correct path and becoming a most perfectly awakened one?
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, excellent!"
O Devaputra of the Yuezhi!

You have great compassion and provide great peace and security; out of pity for the devas and the people of the ten directions, you have been able to resolve to ask the Tathāgata about such a meaning as this.

All these Bodhisattvas who practice the Buddha-way with right and true wisdom, don the great armor, establish the Mahāyāna, cross over great desire, pilot the great ship, and turn the great wheel of Dharma; they bestow the infinite Dharma and propagate the vast scriptures of wisdom. They wish to release a great rain and manifest universal light; they aspire to beat the great drum and resolve upon the thundering of great peals. They delight in erecting the massive banner and vow to blow the great conch; they grasp the flowers of the Great Dharma and take up the scriptures of the Great Dharma.

They expound the infinite radiance, desiring to illuminate the world, and strive to ensure that the Mahāyāna shall exist forever without interruption; they pray that the great sacrificial rites may reach ultimate fulfillment.
By means of these analogies, one may understand his boundless virtue; it is out of compassion for the masses that you have questioned the Tathāgata.
Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well, and I shall explain it to you in detail.

Just as the practice of the great bodhisattvas leads them to attain the great spiritual penetrations and fulfill profound precepts, reaching the unsurpassed, right, and true path to become the most perfectly awakened one.
“Yes, World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear it.
Thus the Devaputra Candraprabha and the great assembly received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha told the devaputra:
"There are four dharmas of practice for a bodhisattva by which one attains the extraordinary conduct of the great noble supernormal powers and crosses over to the other shore.
What are these four?

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva thoroughly understands all phenomena in accordance with the ultimate truth; he has no attachment or reliance upon any phenomenon, maintains an equanimous mindfulness toward all phenomena without exhaustion, attains noble wisdom and achieves clear realization, and dwells within all phenomena while drawing near to the various scriptures.
Although there is no one who attains liberation among all phenomena, one does not perceive any phenomenon that is distinct [from it].
What are these phenomena that correspond to the ultimate truth?
They are as empty as the past; likewise, the future and the present are naturally empty.
"O Son of Heaven!
One who wishes to clearly understand this emptiness and equality [should know that] the three periods of time are empty and devoid of conceptualization.

Those who possess wisdom analyze the various locations, establish and open up the path-factors (*mārga-aṅga*) for liberation, thereby attaining right action and penetrating their underlying principles; this is called clearly understanding and responding to the True Reality (*satya*)."
"What is meant by 'having no attachment or reliance toward any phenomena'?
All phenomena abide within the sphere of 'mine'; yet that which currently appears to abide as 'self' or 'not-self'—the Bodhisattva understands all such phenomena to be devoid of a self.
Not relying upon the body is what is called 'having no attachment or reliance.'"
If a bodhisattva is without attachment toward these dharmas of the body, and having become unattached, does not dwell in any other dharma;
they neither give rise to nor dwell within any dharmas.
If you can have no dependence or attachment toward them, you will already be without dependence;
by making offerings to all dharmas, you will then be without dependence upon those dharmas.
Second, what is meant by a bodhisattva understanding that all things are like empty space?

These three realms are the product of the mind; one should not conceive of this mind as having form or appearance, nor can it be seen. It has no location and no commands, being just like a magical illusion.
If one seeks all phenomena by means of the fundamental nature of the mind, they cannot be found.
If one does not seek the mind within the mind, then there is nothing to be obtained, as the mind cannot be grasped;
since the mind cannot be attained, all phenomena likewise cannot be attained.

All phenomena are devoid of any dharma; they lack the perception of form or category, and being without shadow, they are non-existent; even with regard to ultimate truth, there is nothing to be perceived.
One who has nothing to perceive has no mental entry into any phenomena; they know that all phenomena are unestablished and likewise unarisen.
They are like empty space, O Devaputra!
If one examines empty space, it is eternally without arising and without anything accomplished; one understands that all phenomena are likewise so.
Just as empty space is called "void," it is tranquil and serene.
All dharmas are likewise thus; they are merely provisional designations, for they are ultimately quiescent.
Third, what is meant by a bodhisattva’s intimate engagement with the scriptures regarding all dharmas?
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates and reflects upon all phenomena, there is therein neither cognition nor vision.
The eye does not know the ear, nor does it have any vision; the ear does not know the eye, nor does it have any vision.
The nose does not know the tongue, nor does it have any vision; the tongue does not know the nose, nor does it have any vision.
The body does not know the mind, nor does it have any vision; the mind does not know the body, nor does it have any vision.
Although all phenomena—including ignorance, frivolity, and violence—appear within the dharma-realm, wisdom remains eternally equal, and its practice is fully perfected.

When the realms of the six sense-faculties have something that comes into their illumination, there is a location; yet when one calculates according to the fundamental nature, there are no internal dharmas.
As for that which teaches regarding the external, there are no external dharmas; as for that which teaches regarding internal dharmas, what is seen is thus.
One who perceives in this manner finds that there is no dharma, no one who arises, and no dharma that performs any action;
if there were any abiding, one would perceive nothing at all.
The Buddha said to the devaputra:
"This is the dharma-realm; dharmas neither arise nor cease, and because they do not abide, they are non-existent."
If one should have the thought that all phenomena do not abide, are unarisen, do not originate, and have no location; if one observes in this way,

being fully endowed with the wisdom of ultimate truth, there will be neither phenomena nor a dharma-realm, and one does not perceive liberation— this approaching of all these dharmas through the various scriptures constitutes the four dharmas.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attains the extraordinary practice of the great noble supernormal powers and crosses over to the other shore.
"Fourth, what are the noble supernormal powers?
As for what is called 'supernormal power,' it means that regarding all dharmas, one does not rely on the wisdom of others but possesses the capacity for inquiry and reception."
Therefore, it is said that wisdom does not engage in two things regarding all phenomena; this is what is meant by "non-duality. That which is without name is a phenomenon that cannot be known.
If a son of heaven is fully endowed with this wisdom, that bodhisattva will swiftly attain noble supernormal powers, thereby fulfilling their vows and perfecting all that they understand.
When a bodhisattva clearly understands such wisdom, they purify the eye of the Path and transcend both gods and worldly beings.

They then behold the immeasurable, limitless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of buddha-lands in the ten directions, as well as all the holy assemblies of the Buddhas, the Gods among Gods; they hear all the sūtras and dharmas preached by those Buddhas.

Furthermore, they fully recognize and know the thoughts and intentions—whether good or evil, beautiful or ugly—of the various classes of sentient beings in those buddha-lands, as well as the comings and goings of their people and associates.

Having reached such a state, one knows for oneself the places traversed in the past; through the clear realization of wisdom, one understands the limit of one's own origin, and perceives that other beings have no beginning from which they arose, fully verifying all their dwelling places;
this is spoken according to conditions.
The Buddha told the devaputra:
"Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva has not yet attained all-encompassing omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), his noble and sagely wisdom is as majestic as this.
For the sake of all sentient beings, he establishes the Buddha-work, swiftly fulfills all Buddha-dharmas, and attains the unsurpassed, right, and true path, becoming the Most Perfectly Awakened One."
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“By means of the path of skillful means and the light of wisdom, One fully accomplishes the great sagely penetrations;
Always observing and practicing the profound and wondrous precepts, One immediately uses a single principle to understand all dharmas.”
Discerning all sutras of the ultimate truth, those with clear vision have no attachments;
they constantly contemplate all phenomena as being like emptiness, and through their observation, they proclaim that all things are void.
One practices and draws near to all dharmas, which are merely provisional designations; one does not perceive any dharma that attains liberation.
That which is not perceived is that which nothing fails to observe—such is what is seen by one who has attained noble supernormal powers.
If the dharmas of the past are already empty, then all dharmas of the future are likewise empty;
the analysis of the present is also like this—this is what is called the vision of the ultimate truth.
All phenomena are eternally empty within the three realms; one who clearly understands this has neither thought nor non-thought.
Since there is no longer anything to respond to—neither what is appropriate nor what is inappropriate—one who is thus fearless beholds the True Truth.

If wisdom is thus an expedient of non-attachment, and one expounds the Dharma without the notion of a dharma, the mind has no thoughts and thus nothing to which it clings; that which has nothing to which it clings is unshakable.
All dharmas arise spontaneously; that which is spontaneous is fundamentally pure and without self.
To clearly understand all dharmas as being without "I" or "mine," one then gives rise to nothing else, nor any other dharma.
That which is unborn neither exists nor comes; when one examines and calculates it, there is nothing upon which to rely, yet one still explains the abodes and locations of all dharmas.
Although one expounds the Buddha-way, one does not conceive of a self.
The entire triple world arises from the mind; yet that mind cannot be constantly perceived.
It is formless and devoid of a person, like a magical illusion; one should diligently seek the mind through this very dharma.
Having sought the mind by means of these dharmas, one then knows that there is neither mind nor mental phenomena;
even if one seeks the location of the mind within the mind itself, one will not perceive the fundamental purity of the mind.
Having no attachment to any phenomena, though among the masses, one does not follow after the perceptions of the multitude;
all phenomena are without intention and without accomplishment, always discerned as being like empty space.
Just as one contemplates space as neither arising nor existing, so too is the differentiation of all phenomena;
space is a mere provisional designation and truly lacks substantial reality, for the words used to speak of its existence are themselves empty of that phenomenon.
The eye has never beheld the ear, nor does the ear behold the eye;
the tongue does not belong to the nose, nor does the nose belong to the tongue—these organs, though revolving one after another, do not see each other.
The body has never examined the mind, nor does the mind examine the form and nature of the body.
Each is thus unable to know the other; for this reason, they are eternally tranquil and serene.
Clinging to various evils, flattery, and folly, the realm of all phenomena remains eternally equal and level.
That which pertains to the internal does not know the external, and that which pertains to the external likewise does not know the internal.
For this reason, they understand the course of the Dharma, achieving wisdom that is forever beyond limit.
They behold the billions of Buddhas of the ten directions, as well as their śrāvakas, who are free from all faults;
furthermore, they comprehend the immeasurable, holy, and pure meanings of the sūtras preached by those Buddhas.
They shall fully attain the hearing of the beautiful words that are proclaimed, and thus be able to receive, uphold, and universally practice equanimity.
They will be able to thoroughly understand the mental intentions of sentient beings, and shall possess the power to fly to billions of Buddha-lands,
recollecting the events of countless past ages throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Having attained these five sublime noble superknowledges (*abhijñā*), one then acquires the wisdom of close proximity and stable abiding;
through the Buddha, that which was to be manifested is revealed, and the path of non-negligence brings about beneficial purpose.

If one hears such a teaching on emptiness as this, and gives rise to a heart of exultation, delighting in the subtle and wondrous joy, then Māra shall be unable to find any flaw or shortcoming in them;
they will then be able to swiftly accomplish the realization of the supreme path.
The Buddha told the devaputra:
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva has four dharmas that lead to inconceivable skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*). What are the four?

The Bodhisattva clearly understands the method of coming and going across the stream of existence, regarding it as if it were the various kinds of suffering and poisonous afflictions within his own body, observing how they arise through the course of wandering.

Furthermore, desiring to eliminate the suffering of others, he practices with diligence, exhorts all sentient beings to enter the noble path, and causes them to maintain the aspiration for enlightenment in all phenomena;
he accumulates stores of merit for all the multitudes, remaining thus throughout the three periods of time.

Thus, they encourage and assist all Buddhas, gathering the qualities of virtue from practices throughout the three periods of time; they apply the roots of goodness they have cultivated to sentient beings, and though they practice vast giving and bring about transformation, they do not give rise to a conceptualizing mind.
Regarding that which is not urged forward:
for one who possesses all-knowledge, the mind is neither detached nor does it perceive a path; the mind is not separate from the path, and the path is not separate from the mind.
As is the characteristic of the path, so too is the characteristic of the body.

"By means of wisdom, one maintains equanimity toward the mind and likewise has no dependence upon the Path; following skillful means, one increases and benefits the roots of virtue, yet perceives nothing within the Dharma-realm that is increased."
He does not engage in deliberation regarding any phenomena; he accumulates merit and virtue without ever becoming weary, yet he does not seek to understand the mind through mental activity.

If he practices giving, he is free from expectation; if he observes the precepts, there is nothing lost; if he practices patience, he dwells nowhere; if he exerts diligence, he is free from agitation; if he practices meditative concentration with a single mind, he has no dependence; if he cultivates wisdom, he has nothing to habituate; and in transforming sentient beings, he is free from attachment.
Out of compassion, he adorns and purifies the Buddha-field.
He seeks holy realization without giving rise to longing, and he expounds the Dharma without entering into any [conceptual] state.
"It is thus, O Devaputra!"

Regarding the roots of virtue practiced and cultivated by a bodhisattva, although they may be slight and few, their skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) are immeasurable, leading even to the Great Way (*mahāmārga*).
What is meant by saying that although the roots of virtue cultivated by a bodhisattva are slight and few, through skillful means they attain the immeasurable and reach the Great Way?

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva brings forth immeasurable mindfulness toward all phenomena, they observe that among all phenomena there is none that can be calculated, limited, or reached to its ultimate limit. Why is this so?
"Son of Heaven!
If you wish to know all dharmas, they are empty, without conceptualization, and without aspiration;
that which is empty is likewise immeasurable."
If one has fully mastered the immeasurable mind, then even though the Dharma taught may be slight, the skillful means employed will be vast and boundless. Why is this?
Because the Buddha-way is immeasurable; to encourage the mind toward the infinite and reach the boundless Dharma is the path of all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), exhorts and encourages sentient beings to enter into correct practice.

He observes those among the multitude of living beings who delight in the Dharma and establishes them therein; if there are those to be rescued through giving, he preaches the sūtras and the Dharma for them."
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not regard giving as something definitive, saying: 'This is mine.'"
"Maintaining precepts, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom are likewise not called 'mine.
Furthermore, regarding those who practice giving or maintain the precepts, they have no such thoughts; they always accord with the prohibitions and precepts.
They are fully endowed with patience, and when seeing the actions of others, whether right or wrong, they endure them all."
Practice with diligence, cultivate pure conduct;
maintain single-minded meditative reflection;
master skillful means, and observe with wisdom.
"Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva clearly discerns and understands:
though he employs skillful means (upāya-kauśalya) to associate with and transform Śrāvakas, he does not take delight in their practice."
Their cultivation is steadfast as they associate with pratyekabuddhas; they take no pleasure in their own [limited] practices and fortify their resolve.
These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains inconceivable skillful means (upāyakauśalya).
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Clearly understanding these two matters— One's own self and others—
One should eliminate one's own suffering and affliction, And cure all the burning fevers of the multitude."
Out of compassion for sentient beings, you urge them toward the mind of the Way;
contemplating all phenomena, you expound them so they may enter into the single meaning.
All living beings rejoice as these [teachings] are gathered together throughout the three periods of time.
One should universally exhort and transform others regarding the virtues of all Buddhas;
understanding them all thoroughly, one bestows them upon sentient beings,
giving with a sincere heart because of the wisdom of the Buddha.
All the minds they have generated, they entirely exhort toward the Buddha-way;
Without losing the mind of the Way, they see all dharmas as completely liberated.
Examining the mind and the Way, they do not perceive these two things as distinct.
Its characteristics have that which remains; one thoroughly understands that the characteristics of the mind are equal.
Because dharmas are equal, they are impartial; non-dual and non-existent, one clearly knows the provisional skillful means, thereby perpetually increasing the pure and white dharmas.
Its lineage is of unconditioned benefit; the Dharma-realm is beyond conceptualization.
Resolutely seeking the Buddha-way, one is always free from weariness.
Not using the mind to contemplate the mind, I maintain a long-standing reputation for purity.
Never forgetting the mind of the Way, they encourage and assist all that is done.
They practice giving without expecting reward, maintain the precepts without conceptualization,
constantly cultivate patience, and do not establish the notion of a person.
Constantly practicing with diligence, body, speech, and mind are tranquil;
in meditative concentration there is no dependence, and wisdom is the perfection of the infinite.
Opening the way for liberation, they transform sentient beings, never dwelling in perversion.
He purifies all Buddha-fields, and his nature is free from rigidity.
Always intent upon the Buddha-way, he relinquishes nothing of the Dharma;
having consulted and received all scriptures, his wisdom is beyond measure.
They preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, Without attachment to words and letters.
One who practices in this manner Will swiftly attain Buddhahood without difficulty.
Their mind does not dwell on emptiness, It is free from pride and devoid of discursive thought.
Without conceptualization and without aspiration, immeasurable and beyond limit;
knowing the conduct of all beings, he transforms them accordingly;
acting with sovereign mastery, he practices giving and preaches the Dharma to provide for their lack.
There is one who gives to sentient beings, yet does not say "I have gained [merit]";
who is not arrogant regarding precepts, nor neglectful of patience; who is not indolent toward diligence, nor attached to meditative concentration;
and who, regarding wisdom, has no sense of stinginess.
Always delighting in giving and discussing the various precepts, he follows and cultivates humility, constantly practicing with vigor.
Although he honors meditative reflection, he is forever free from attachment;
he gives rise to wisdom and practices it through generosity.
Whether among pratyekabuddhas or śrāvakas, or as bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wandering among such ranks—
if one should dwell therein and perform any karmic actions, the wise one with clear vision does not delight in such conduct.
One who is able to establish such a Dharma as this is what is called the practice of a bodhisattva.
Understanding skillful means that are inconceivable, their acts of giving reach the limitlessness of the infinite.
The Buddha told the devaputra:
"A bodhisattva has four dharmas.
All phenomena are treated as a single discourse; they enter into a single flavor where their destination is equal, and they enter into the teaching of the equality of a single wisdom."
What are these four?
A bodhisattva mahāsattva clearly understands that the dharma-realm is indestructible; he realizes the emptiness of all phenomena and wanders everywhere therein.

Regarding the discourse on all phenomena, he perceives no distinguishing marks; he regards himself and others with equanimity; and he clearly understands that all phenomena are entirely tranquil. These are the four.

“Clearly understanding that what is perceived by wisdom is thus, one attains thorough penetration into both mundane and supramundane dharmas, yet does not construct dualistic views—whether of sin or merit, obstruction or non-obstruction, hearing or not hearing, conditioned or unconditioned.
Regarding all these dharmas, one neither constructs nor observes them, and sees no dharma whatsoever that can be grasped.”

There is no dharma of ordinary persons, nor any dharma of arhats; there is no manifold contemplation, for the dharma of ordinary persons is not rendered pure, nor is the dharma of arhats examined as being uniquely enlightened.
Without elevating or disparaging, they distinguish the single principle, proceeding toward the gate of tranquility to expound and explain it.
They disperse all phenomena, yet perceive no dispersal or destruction within those phenomena;
they practice a singular forbearance that is forever non-dual, thereby entering the single principle and universally penetrating all dharmas.
What is called "entering" has no point of origin.
It is thus, O Son of Heaven!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva draws near to the unsurpassed, right, and true path and attains supreme perfect enlightenment, he likewise does not harbor the thought:
"Whether I am near or far.
Why is this? Because one does not abide in a single fixed position.
Seeing the various multitudes of beings, he also observed that persons and the Way are distinct from one another.
Furthermore, he reflected that a person cannot be apprehended; such is the Way.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"And within the dharma-realm, there is nothing to be destroyed; furthermore, that dharma-realm cannot be dispersed by anyone.
Considering the dharma-realm to be such, all people are likewise: they exist only as provisional designations, and there is no plurality."
Having realized that all phenomena are empty, one attains the patience of non-arising;

whether internal or external, conditioned or unconditioned—observing these dharmas, one finds they are entirely non-existent. By analyzing them through a single principle, one knows them all to be empty.
All phenomena that appear have no common likeness; one does not cling to oneself nor to others.
If one does not harbor thoughts of "I," "mine," "person," or "self," then in their practice there will never be any manifold conceptualizations.
Cultivating profound stillness, with the mind intent on serene detachment, one universally contemplates the existence of all phenomena.
Regarding all dharmas, one remains tranquil and silent, free from discursive thought; wandering in serene detachment, one is without any attachment.
When preaching about the present or matters concerning the world, he does not give rise to them; he brings about their exhaustion and utter cessation.
Whether it be merit or sin, whether heard or unheard, he does not dwell upon dharmas nor grasp at sounds.
Not abiding in the conditioned, nor in the unconditioned, one constantly maintains the single contemplation and takes no delight in these two matters.
Not perceiving any phenomena that can be grasped, one finds neither the ordinary person nor the Arhat.
One does not speak of ordinary people as being deluded, defiled, or impure; this is what is called the Dharma of the Arhat.
There is nothing to be exalted and nothing to be disparaged; all conceptual distinctions are entirely quiescent.
To clearly understand that all phenomena are entirely indestructible, and neither to be disintegrated nor dispersed throughout the entire dharma-realm—is this not what is called patience?
Is it not distinct from emptiness?
Universally knowing that all phenomena are entirely empty;
not clinging to emptiness, one attains the realization of patience through non-reliance, thereby entering the single principle and fully comprehending all things.
This has no arising; its essence is fundamentally pure. A practitioner who acts in this way will swiftly attain the Buddha-way.
They will quickly draw near to the immeasurable Perfectly Awakened Ones, neither reckoning the existence of a body nor dwelling on the thought of a bodhicitta.
"In all dharmas, there is no attachment whatsoever to self or to others; thus one attains equal enlightenment.
The Buddha told the devaputra:
"A bodhisattva has four dharmas by which they uphold profound precepts and practice without negligence."
What are the four?
The bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects to himself:
"What is meant by the prohibitive precepts?"
Then, he proceeded to observe and contemplate this principle:
"If one's bodily actions are good, one's speech is sincere, and one's mental thoughts are gentle and compliant, this constitutes the prohibitive precepts."
Furthermore, he thought to himself:
"What is meant by goodness of body?
What is meant by sincerity of speech?"
"What is meant by a supple mind?
It is not committing physical misdeeds—namely, refraining from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; this is the cultivation of goodness in bodily action.
It is not speaking what is wrong with the mouth—namely, refraining from lying, divisive speech, harsh words, and slanderous talk; this is sincerity in verbal expression."
When the mind does not dwell on what is improper, but dwells instead on matters of anger and wrong views, this is the mind dwelling in softness.
He observes with discernment and reflects to himself:

"If one does not transgress in body, speech, or mind, one cannot distinguish the locations where [colors] such as blue, yellow, red, white, purple, or crimson reside; even when considering the eye, one does not conceptually differentiate consciousness."
The ear, nose, mouth, and mind are likewise; they do not engage in discriminative consciousness.
Why is this? They neither arise nor is there one who causes them to arise; they neither originate nor is there one who causes them not to originate.
"If there were no arising and nothing that arose, there would likewise be no origination;
and where there is no origination, one is incapable of discerning and cognizing phenomena.
He then further reflected:
"At that time, when one examines it, there is nothing whatsoever.
Since there is no precept, there is no practice;
since there is no practice, it cannot be known."
Since it is already unknowable, one should not have any dependence or attachment toward it; having performed this practice, there is nothing to be seen.
At that time, one does not see precepts;
since one does not see precepts, one also does not see anyone who encourages those precepts.
This, O Devaputra,
is how a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva upholds the profound prohibitions and precepts.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra:"

If there is a bodhisattva who understands the non-attachment to the body, who does not dwell upon the perception of the body nor perceive the cultivation of precepts, who neither violates prohibitions nor has any attachment.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva enters the profound treasury of the Dharma, he maintains the prohibitions under his protection, observes dignified deportment and ritual propriety, and moves with a calm and composed gait that accords with the teachings; this is called morality (śīla).
Not seeing one's own arising conduct, and not seeing the faults of others—for this reason, it is called the profound and wondrous precept.
"Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!
A bodhisattva does not transgress the precepts, nor does he violate them, nor does he play with them.
For one who turns back from himself, there is a turning back from the precepts;
if one does not turn back from himself, then there is no turning back from the precepts, and because there is no turning back from the precepts, there is nothing to be transgressed.
Having already not transgressed the precepts, one does not toy with them, and thus there is nothing further to be delivered.
The reason one neither toys with nor delivers the precepts is that one realizes all dharmas are already fully delivered and liberated.
Because those who are delivered and liberated possess neither a self nor a non-self.
Since there is no person, who is it that is delivered?
These are the four.
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"His body is pure, his speech is free from error, his thoughts are clear, and his conduct is without blemish;
he constantly guards himself and is prudent in his actions."
That bodhisattva is said to be one who upholds the precepts.

Regarding these ten wholesome actions, if an intelligent bodhisattva can protect them, then their body, speech, and mind will be free from transgression; this can truly be called [upholding the precepts].
I respectfully uphold the clear and penetrating precepts.
They have no form or color, nor do they have a location;
since they are already without appearance, they abide nowhere. Being thus ungraspable, where could they possibly go?
The precepts are without fabrication and are always like the unconditioned;
thus, they cannot be observed with the eye.
There is nothing heard by the ear, no nose, no tongue, and the body cannot distinguish them, nor can they be conceived by the mind.
If one does not engage in conceptual discrimination regarding the six sense faculties, then one will penetrate all realms of existence without any dependence or reliance.
If one contemplates in this way, that is the pure precept; it is a precept that has never been attained as something established upon a fixed basis.
He possesses no attachment to precepts; he is without conceptualization or fixed correctness. He guards the prohibitions and precepts, yet has no notion of a self.
He nurtures the prohibitions without even the thought of "precepts," cultivating the profound and essential precepts until his will attains mastery.
Because one is able to discern that which is seen as the body,
one does not fall into the sixty-two doubts.
When there is nothing seen and no place perceived, although one observes the prohibitions and precepts, one does not become self-conceited or indulgent.
Thus one can accord with and enter the profound and wondrous treasury of the Dharma; the rites and decorum one practices are free from false conceptualization.
One skillfully cultivates composure and tranquility, following with prudence and care; as for these prohibitions and precepts, there is no attachment to difference.
Not leaning on a self, nor relying on the precepts; having no self, there are then no prohibitions or rules.
Not thinking of one's own body, nor of the prohibitions and rules—it is only in this way that one is called a vessel for the Dharma.
One who has no sense of self does not rely upon precepts; one who does not reckon the body does not conceptualize dharmas.
One who is free from the view of a body has no mind fixated on precepts.
One who does not violate the precepts has no transgression of the prohibitions.
Furthermore, they do not establish themselves within the prohibitions; by not reckoning the existence of a self, they have no notion of "precepts."
The profound and subtle precepts are said to be those where nothing is transgressed;
if one is courageous and observes the precepts in this manner, then one has never committed any violation.
Such precepts as these are praised by the noble and the wise; regarding all phenomena, they are without attachment.
The foolish and deluded person dwells in the notion of a self and, while observing the prohibitions and precepts, says, "I am cautious and fearful."
Then one loses the jewel of the precepts, leaving nothing remaining forever; consequently, one shall not be delivered from the afflictions of the three realms.
Suppose there were a person who removes the net of all views; such a person would not be seen to violate or lose the prohibitive precepts.
By faithfully observing the prohibitions and precepts, one does not fall into views of doubt;
thus, one will not fear falling into the evil realms.
If one were to discriminate in this way regarding the precepts, then one would not perceive those who violate the prohibitions and precepts.
They do not examine self or other, nor do they perceive the three periods of time; how much less could they observe or refrain from violating the precepts and destroying the prohibitions?
The Devaputra Candraprabha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is unprecedented, O God among Gods!"
The path and Dharma of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are subtle and wondrous; they are unsurpassed, truly correct, profoundly deep, and difficult to fathom.

The deeds performed by Bodhisattvas are foremost and most majestic, for they are able to reverently cultivate such a Dharma while abiding nowhere and practicing nothing, having eliminated all false conceptualizations and being free from thoughts of self.

Practicing through incalculable kalpas, they do not fall back into the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, nor do they midway deviate from or lose their resolve for the Way; they fulfill the Buddha-dharma and enter into it without deficiency or leakage.
"How does a bodhisattva practice which dharmas and cultivate the subtle and wondrous scriptures so as not to realize the ultimate limit of reality?
The World-Honored One replied,
"Listen, Son of Heaven!
There are four practices by which a bodhisattva cultivates the profound and wondrous Dharma, yet does not realize the ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi).
What are these four?

First, the bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses firm resolve and establishes essential practices, being endowed with all-knowledge (sarvajñā) and practicing diligence without cowardice. Second, they do not abide in [nirvāṇa] while failing to abandon sentient beings. Third, they do not sever the teaching of great compassion (mahākaruṇā). Fourth, through skillful means (upāyakauśalya), they exhort others toward the roots of merit (kuśalamūla).
"These are the four practices of the profound and wondrous Dharma, by which one does not realize the ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi) prematurely.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The wise person, whose resolve is firm and strong, never deviates from it."
That which was understood in the past constitutes all-knowledge;
through diligent and earnest cultivation, one ultimately does not abide in the rise or fall of divergent vehicles.
Always free from negligence, they dare to follow and practice;
their minds are neither timid nor weak, nor do they ever abandon any sentient being.
With a mind of universal equanimity toward all classes of living beings, he constantly extends compassion to the multitudes throughout the world.
Able to endure diligent toil, his resolve never wavers; his aspiration is not to allow the Way and its teachings to be severed.
He is well-awakened and understands thoroughly; through skillful means and expedient methods, he encourages all virtues and practices them without weariness.
He pursues the most essential path, cherishing compassion, and does not extinguish all outflows in the interim.
Those who have received the transmission of this sutra, those bodhisattvas are named "The Valiant.
They constantly practice and cultivate the profound and wondrous Dharma, yet they never rely upon or cling to the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
The Devaputra Candraprabha again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva practicing the profound and essential?
The Buddha told the devaputra:
"In this regard, the Bodhisattva never destroys the dharmas of ordinary beings, yet universally accomplishes the discourse on the Buddha-way.
He neither slanders nor毁 (destroys) the dharmas of ordinary beings,
nor does he perceive the Buddhadharma as something that increases."
Nor do they distance themselves from the dharmas of ordinary beings,
nor do they seek them with longing.
One who wishes to attain the Buddha-way does not engage in such conduct, for is the dharma of ordinary beings one thing and the Buddha-way another?
Nor does one think:
"The dharmas of ordinary beings are flawed, defiled, and base;
whereas the Way and Dharma of the Buddha are subtle and wondrous?"
"If one does not practice in this way, the dharmas of ordinary persons will become these outflows; yet, in the Dharma of the Buddha, are there no such leaks?
Furthermore, he thought again:
"The dharmas of ordinary persons and the dharmas of the Buddha—both are dharmas that are empty, non-existent, and tranquil; they are merely provisional designations!"
Thought leads to defilement.
The dharmas of ordinary beings are not accomplished;
the dharmas of the Buddhas are not fully possessed.
The dharmas of ordinary beings have no reality and possess no intrinsic nature;
the dharmas of all Buddhas likewise have no reality and possess no intrinsic nature.
If one seeks the principle, the dharmas of ordinary beings are neither known nor unknown, and are neither produced nor unproduced.

If an observer investigates its beginning and end, using the wisdom of emptiness, the wisdom of signlessness, and the wisdom of wishlessness, such clear and discerning wisdom is what constitutes the Buddha-dharma.
One cannot separately know the locus of the Buddha-dharma; when one contemplates its beginning and end, all of it is empty.
In emptiness, one does not perceive emptiness; there is neither that which is known nor that which is observed. All is fundamentally pure, yet it arises due to ignorance.
"Therefore, O Son of Heaven!
The Dharma is non-dharmic; all dharmas abide spontaneously, and all dharmas are serene.
That serene dharma is without duality."

In that state of non-duality, there are no ordinary beings, nor śrāvakas, nor pratyekabuddhas; it is the equal path of the Buddha, wherein there is no teaching of profound and subtle practices for the conduct of a bodhisattva.
When a bodhisattva deeply cultivates the discernment of the true teaching, there is not a single dharma that is not the Buddha-dharma. Why is this?
That which is called "dharma" refers to worldly conventions as dharma; yet, there are no words of worldly convention [in the ultimate sense].
That which is spoken has nothing that can be attained;
where there is nothing attained, there is nothing that arises.
Because nothing arises, there is no teaching of form; all dharmas are entirely devoid of form or image.
Even if all phenomena were without limit or number, they would not be apart from the Buddha-dharma.
"Therefore, O Son of Heaven,
you should form this contemplation:
All dharmas are entirely the Buddha-dharma, devoid of conceptualization and volitional activity (*saṃskāra*).
Any such conceptualization or volitional activity immediately gives rise to the consciousness of the two matters of arising and ceasing.
Beings of this sort take consciousness as their practice.
The Buddha-dharma is without outflows, yet one does not conceive of or seek it therein; therein arises the practice of the śrāvaka.
One who understands this realizes that the dharma-realm is neither defiled nor quiescent.
If one does not grasp at dharmas within the dharma, then there are no dharmas.
How could the dharmas of affliction and the dharma of tranquility be attained as either affliction or tranquility?
"If one seeks to act in this way, it can ultimately not be attained. Thus, O Devaputra,
if a bodhisattva understands in this manner, it is called 'profound and wondrous practice.'"
Regarding all phenomena and the Buddha-dharma, those who have no perception are, by virtue of having no perception, free from views;
that which they perceive is non-perception.
"If a bodhisattva contemplates in this manner, Māra and his retinue will be unable to find an opportunity, nor will they be able to overcome him.
*The Sutra on the Buddha Ascending to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Preach the Dharma for His Mother*, Scroll One;
*The Sutra on the Buddha Ascending to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Preach the Dharma for His Mother*, Scroll Two.
The Moon-Clan Devaputra addressed the Buddha, saying: "Indeed, World-Honored One! This is most unprecedented."

The conduct of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is difficult to fathom; observing all phenomena in such a manner, he remains intent upon their ultimate destination, yet throughout the beginning and end, death and birth, sitting and rising, and even speech, he is free from any conceptualization.
The Buddha said:
"For example, O Son of Heaven!
It is like a conjurer’s magical creation that comes and goes, moves about, sits, stands, and walks, and even utters instructions, yet it has no conceptual thought."
Thus it is, O Devaputra!
Those who clearly understand that all phenomena are like illusions, appearing universally throughout the five destinies yet without being born, are without conceptualization.
Such Bodhisattvas do not dwell on birth nor give rise to anything; yet, by virtue of their original vows, they establish themselves and manifest as being born.
The devaputra asked again:
“As Your Reverence has taught, you say:
‘A bodhisattva does not conceive thoughts of birth, nor does he undergo rebirth.’”

"How is it that the Great Sage, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, out of compassion and mindful of his biological kin, ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven for three months at one time? Did the Tathāgata not actually take birth from Queen Māyā?"
The Buddha told the devaputra:
"A bodhisattva is not born from Queen Māyā; he should always accord with the Dharma.
The devaputra asked again:
“Tathāgata, Arhat!
How does one arise?
The Buddha said:
“Son of Heaven!
The Tathāgata is born from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
If one were to examine and investigate its source and its end, among all the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, who could be said to be his mother?”
One should then comprehend this: the Perfection of Wisdom is its mother!
Why is that? O Son of Heaven!
These thirty-two marks of a great man are not produced from Māyā;
rather, by studying the meaning of the true reality of great wisdom, one is able to attain this, naturally accomplishing the body of a Tathāgata.
As for those ten powers, they were not born from Queen Māyā.
Originally, by practicing the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā), he attained the ten powers;
likewise, the four fearlessnesses and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha were also not born from Queen Māyā.

Great kindness and great compassion; the invisible crown of the head and the unfailing vision; the Buddha-eye, the Buddha-wisdom, and the Buddha’s eloquence; knowing the origins from which the thoughts of people arise; the supernormal powers and skillful means—such as these are immeasurable, all resulting from the boundless transcendence through wisdom.
Therefore, the Tathāgata is named "Buddha"; all these merits were not born from Queen Māyā.
"Son of Heaven!

You should know that they all arise from training in this path-factor through the practice of the Great Perfection of Wisdom (Mahāprajñāpāramitā). It is because of this that the Tathāgata attains such a form, the immeasurable Buddha-dharmas, and the vast virtues of a Tathāgata; for this reason, he is called the Tathāgata."
Therefore, O Son of Heaven!
You should form this view:
the Tathāgata is born from the perfection of wisdom; he is not born of Queen Māyā.
The devaputra asked again:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
The Dharma of the Perfection of Wisdom has no mother; it neither arises nor ceases."
"How is it, World-Honored One?
How does the Tathāgata arise from the Perfection of Wisdom?
The Buddha said:
“Devaputra! It is because of that Dharma that he is called the Tathāgata.
That Dharma has neither arising nor cessation; it is neither born nor extinguished.”
That which has neither arising nor passing away is neither produced nor extinguished.
This formless dharma is born from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); for this reason, it is said that the perfection of wisdom gives birth to the Tathāgata.
That which is produced is entirely without production, nor does it perish; furthermore, there is no arising.
The Buddha said, “Devaputra!
That which is neither born nor perishes, neither arises nor ceases—this is called the locus of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Although the perfection of wisdom appears as if it were born and as if it were active, the perfection of wisdom has never been born, nor does it have any activity.
The devaputra asked again:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
Wisdom possesses ideation and possesses discrimination.”
"Yet, relying on wisdom, they act as if something were being produced and as if something were being performed.
The Buddha said,
"Devaputra!"
Wisdom is without conceptualization and without discrimination.
If wisdom were to involve conceptualization or discrimination, it would not be performing the work of wisdom.
Why is this? For one who has conceptualizations or views, it is not the proper practice.
If, regarding wisdom, one has no thoughts and no discriminations, that can be called the practice of wisdom.
He asked again:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by ‘practice based on reliance’?”
He replied: "O Devaputra!
For one who relies on practice, there is nothing to be grasped through speech; upon what, then, could they rely?"
The Buddha said to the devaputra:
"One who takes up [the teaching] without words thereby relinquishes that which is born within the triple world.
One who takes up it through words, however, does not depart from that which is born within the triple world."
Therefore, O Son of Heaven!
I have merely expounded this teaching.
Since there is no speech, upon what could one rely for practice, such that one would give rise to the three realms and find something to rely upon?
The devaputra asked again:
"How does the World-Honored One preach the Dharma for the śrāvakas to deliver them across the three realms?
The Buddha told the devaputra:
"I preach the Dharma for the sake of the śrāvakas based on the causes and conditions of the desire realm.
Furthermore, although the Tathāgata’s body does not belong to the desire realm, he expounds the sūtras for the sake of the śrāvakas within the form and formless realms."
The Tathāgata does not apprehend a dwelling place in the realm of form or the formless realm, nor is there anything for him to transcend; yet the assembly of śrāvakas transcends the realm of desire.
The Buddha likewise does not apprehend the realms of form or the formless, yet the assembly of śrāvakas surmounts and transcends them, emerging from the realms of form and the formless.
Furthermore, O Devaputra!

One does not grasp the three realms nor rely upon the three realms; one reckons the dharmas of emptiness and gentleness, does not conform to the desire realm, and harbors no longing within the three realms.
"Though born within the triple world, there is nothing that is born, nor does one know where one goes.
O Son of Heaven!
If you wish to know what is meant by 'crossing over,' it is this:"
The teaching of the worthy and holy is merely provisional speech!
When one pursues it through ultimate right principle, there is no measure; there is neither going nor returning. Why is this so?
One contemplates all phenomena as having no one who crosses over.
They are like space, ultimately natural, without anything born and nothing to which one is attached;
without an agent and without anything existing, yet not non-existent either.
"One should contemplate all phenomena in this very same way.
When the World-Honored One had spoken these words, seventy-two thousand deities from that assembly attained the Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena, free from dust and removed from defilement.
Sixteen thousand devaputras, having planted the roots of merit in past lives, all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
One thousand bodhisattvas, having fully perfected the roots of merit, attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, flowers spontaneously appeared upon their robes—something that had never occurred before.
Each took these flowers to make offerings to the Tathāgata; at that moment, those flowers were spread everywhere throughout the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have never before seen such noble sons of good family as these who revere the Tathāgata.
The Devaputra Candrasūrya replied to Śakra, Lord of Devas:
“Kauśika! Listen for a moment.
As for these flowers now scattered upon the Tathāgata, no one among the multitude has ever before beheld such a Holy Honored One.”
Why is this? That mind by which one perceives the Tathāgata has suddenly passed away and ceased, and thus cannot be seen.
Therefore, Kauśika!
"Regarding that which is seen: all dharmas are fundamentally empty, and thus fundamentally unseen.
Kauśika asked again:
"O Devaputra!"
"Do you now see the Tathāgata? He replied, "I do."
Kauśika, observe this!
If the Tathāgata possessed form or were conditioned, then one would indeed see him.
If the Tathāgata possessed feeling, perception, mental formations, volitional consciousness, or discernment, then I would see him.
The Tathāgata has no form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; he is without conjunction and without anything that exists.
Regarding the conceptualization of the five aggregates as dharmas, there is no such conceptualization, and he cannot be viewed through form.
Furthermore, as for what Kauśika said just now:
"Do you see the Tathāgata?
If the Tathāgata were to see my body, my beholding the Tathāgata would likewise be exactly so.
He asked again:
"O Son of Heaven!
How does the Tathāgata perceive such a body as yours?"
The devaputra replied,
“Since the Tathāgata is present before you, you may now pose your question.
Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, stepped forward and addressed the Buddha:
“How does the Blessed One perceive the devaputra? The Blessed One replied, “I do not perceive him by means of form;
nor do I perceive him by means of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.”
One does not perceive the past, the future, or the present; nor does one perceive the dharmas of ordinary beings, yet one is not separated from the dharmas of ordinary beings.
One does not perceive what is learned or what is not learned, nor does one learn to achieve the ultimate realization of all dharmas.
One does not perceive the dharma of an Arhat, nor does one perceive a Śrāvaka, nor does one perceive the stage of a Pratyekabuddha, for there is no such stage of a Pratyekabuddha.
Such is what the Buddha perceives.
To cultivate this contemplation is to engage in right contemplation;
yet for one who engages in right contemplation, there is nothing perceived.
That which is without seeing is the contemplation of equality; it is not a perverse contemplation. "Kauśika!
If you wish to know the contemplation of the Tathāgata, it is exactly like this, no different."
One who contemplates in this manner perceives all things universally; this is called "thorough contemplation of all.
For this reason, the Tathāgata is named Buddha, for that which the Tathāgata brings forth does not destroy the dharma-realm.
"What do you think?
When the Tathāgata perceives such dharmas as these, what is it that he perceives?
He replied:
“World-Honored One!
Thus the Tathāgata does not perceive a name or title, nor is there any form.
Regarding what is thus observed, there is no enumeration of dharmas and nothing that is produced.”
He asked again:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
Is it as the Buddha perceives it that the Devaputra Candraprabha perceives it?"
He replied: "Kauśika!

Those bodhisattva practitioners who have attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) and who dwell in accordance with the realm of all phenomena (dharmadhātu)—for them, no phenomenon perceives a phenomenon; thus there is nothing whatsoever, for it is the spontaneously present dharma."
He asked again:
"World-Honored One,
has the Devaputra Candraprabha attained the patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti)?"
The Buddha told Kauśika:
"Ask the Devaputra Candraka yourself; he shall provide the answer.
Thereupon, the Lord of Devas questioned Candraka:
“O Benevolent One!
Have you attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena?
The Devaputra replied:
"Kauśika, in your opinion, can there be an origination from that which is unarisen? He replied, "No!"
He replied:
"If there is no arising from anything, there is no origination.
How, then, can one attain the patience toward the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti)?"
"This refers to the fact that the entire dharma-realm is entirely without arising.
As for this dharma-realm, it neither arises nor ceases, and it is likewise unattainable.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, thought to himself:

"Now that the Son of Heaven has something to expound, does he consider this as having attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and as being in close proximity to the unsurpassed, right, and true Way?"
The Devaputra Candraprabha, immediately knowing the thoughts in the mind of Śakra, replied to the Lord of Devas:
"Kauśika! One who wishes to attain the patience of the Dharma does not practice for the sake of drawing near to the Unsurpassed, Right, and True Path."
"One who possesses the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena is able to draw near to the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
He asked again:
"O Son of Heaven!"
"Why is this said? He replied:
"Those who have something to attain fall into inversion; yet there is also nothing to be attained."
As for that mind of the Way, there is no realization of awakening nor the non-arising of patience; this is called "that which is nowhere born.
That which does not arise is precisely what constitutes the attainment of perfect awakening.
He asked again:
"O Son of Heaven!
Where should the Way be sought?"
He replied: "Kauśika!
As for that mind of the Way, one should seek it naturally within one's own person."
He asked again:
"As for that which is natural within one's own person, where should it be sought?
He replied:
"That Dharma is unborn; there is neither one who gives birth nor anything that is born. One should seek it therein.
One should cultivate this seeking, seeking as one seeks the mind, not seeking for reputation, and having nothing sought;
when there is nothing sought, there is no abiding."
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, came forward and addressed the Buddha:
“It is truly unprecedented, O God among Gods!
The Son of Heaven from the Moon Realm has entered deeply into wisdom that is lofty and boundless. From where did he pass away to come and be born here?”
"Having passed away from here, where will they be reborn?
The Devaputra Candraprabha replied to Śakra, Lord of Devas:
"Suppose a conjurer were to produce a magical transformation; would it be male or female?"
"From where did he pass away to come and be born here?
Having passed away from this state, where will he go next?
He replied:
“An emanation has no destination to which it goes.
Furthermore, that which is an emanation has neither death nor birth. Why is this so?
"A transformation has no perception. He replied, "Kauśika!
If there were no such thing as non-conceptualization, how could it be that this illusory person goes to that place, passes away from there to be born here,
and having passed away from here, is to be born in such-and-such a place?
"To entertain such a thought is not the mark of one who is wise, and it will be an object of ridicule for others.
He replied, "So it is, O Devaputra!"
It is exactly as you have said.
What Kūṭadanta has now asked is likewise so:
all dharmas are entirely like illusions, yet he asks the Tathāgata about them.
"From where did this devaputra pass away to be reborn here?
Having passed away from there, to what realm did he go? What do you think?
"How could that which is conjured by illusion have coming or going? How could its passing away or being born ever be perceived? He replied, "No!"
"Regarding that which is transformed by causes, is there anything it intends to initiate or anything it intends to create?
He replied,
"There is nothing created."
He replied: "It is so!
One who thoroughly understands that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations is able to manifest going and coming, as well as passing away and being born."
Although he manifests these things, he has no conceptualization and performs no action.
What do you think?

If one sees forms in a dream, or hears sounds, smells odors with the nose, tastes flavors with the mouth, experiences tactile sensations with the body, or cognizes mental phenomena with the mind—can these be said to truly exist as substantial entities?
He replied, “No! The devaputra answered:

"So it is, Kauśika! One who clearly understands that all phenomena are like dreams and like *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature)—whatever they see or hear, their mind is unstained by any phenomena; they neither distance themselves from defilements, nor do they have anything to seek, nor do they feel sorrow or distress."
"Having analyzed all the teachings as they have been heard, one explains them for others;
yet, one remains unattached even to the sounds of speech.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
Since the Devaputra Candraprabha has not attained birth, and neither perishes nor is born, by what means should he transform and guide sentient beings?”
The multitudes of living beings have birth and they have death and extinction; yet in the stage of the śrāvaka, there is neither birth nor death.

Since neither birth nor death is the stage of the bodhisattva, how could the practice of a bodhisattva involve remaining within birth and death to roam for countless hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas?
The Buddha told Śakra, Lord of Devas:

"There are bodhisattvas who have attained and accomplished the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti); they do not conceive of birth, nor is there for them any passing away, just as if an arhat had been in parinirvāṇa for a hundred years."
Why is this? The observation of a bodhisattva is also like this:
a bodhisattva has no notion of self and no notion of others.

The conduct of the Bodhisattva further surpasses even that; he does not dwell on thoughts of birth, nor does he harbor notions of ending or passing away. He is free from the notions of "self" and "other," for all have attained parinirvāṇa.
All dharmas have neither beginning nor end.
If one does not understand these dharmas, there will be nothing to be awakened to.

The Bodhisattva of Great Compassion, even if he were to spend countless eons—hundreds, thousands, tens of millions, and billions—wandering through the cycle of birth and death, would never grow weary.
For example, it is like a man who, having burned down a great house at a crossroads, has no further attachment to it.
One who practices great compassion is likewise: they do not begrudge their own body or life.
Regarding the five pleasures, they cast them aside and abandon all that is desired, as if staying far from a great fire;
though remaining amidst the fire, they are able to endure it all, and their bodies are not burned.
"What do you think?
Is what that person has done difficult?
He replied:
"It is most difficult,
O God among Gods!
the Buddha said.
"Kauśika! The conduct of a bodhisattva exceeds even this.
Having transcended all the defilements of desire, they manifest birth in order to teach and transform the multitudes."
Therefore, one should contemplate this:
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva transcends all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, attains the unsurpassed, right, and true path, and becomes the Most Perfectly Awakened One.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, Lord of Devas:
"Just now, you asked:
'From where did you pass away to be born here?'"
"Listen to what the Buddha says:
ninety-two billion hundred-thousand buddha-fields to the east of here, there is a world named Accumulated Jewels (*Ratnasaṃcaya*).
In that land, there are countless trees made of various jewels; their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits are each distinct and different."
The walkways, pavilions, and lecture halls for viewing and strolling were all made of the seven treasures.
The ground of that land was entirely of deep blue lapis lazuli, composed of countless hundreds of thousands of various jewels.
In the world-system called Accumulated Jewels, there dwells a Buddha named Jewel-Throne Majestic Transcendent King Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently resides there preaching the Dharma.

In that Buddha-land, there are no teachings or practices of the two vehicles of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; it is entirely composed of Bodhisattvas who are fully endowed with vast and universal qualities, filling the entire Buddha-field.
When that Buddha preached the Dharma in a single assembly, thirty-six billion bodhisattvas attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).

As soon as the multitude had attained this patience, they immediately leaped into the air to a height of four *zhang* and nine *chi*, causing the trichiliocosm to tremble. Then, countless hundreds of thousands of lotuses made of the seven precious gems naturally spread across the ground, covering it entirely without exception.

He immediately departed from the void to travel to another buddha-field, where he paid his respects to the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One of that foreign land; bowing his head in refuge, he inquired about the Dharma of the sutras and listened to the meaning of what was taught.
That Buddha has appeared for twelve kalpas, preaching the Dharma three times each day and night.
For this reason, Kauśika,
you should form this understanding.
In that Buddha’s realm, the assembly of bodhisattvas is incalculable in the hundreds of millions; there is no depletion, and various treasures are amassed.
In that Buddha-land, there are no names for other congregations, nor are there mountains, forests, valleys, or deep abysses.
There are none who engage in idle talk, nor are there any afflictions, arhats, or pratyekabuddhas; there are no beings who consume food or drink.
Why is this? These bodhisattvas have long taken the joy of delighting in the Dharma as their sustenance.
Now this devaputra has passed away from the world of Accumulated Jewels and come to this place, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

Therefore, he has come to see the Buddha, prostrate himself, take refuge, and inquire about the sūtras, so that for countless people you may expound this sūtra-dharma and extensively explain its meaning.
Furthermore, he wishes to cause all other bodhisattvas to fully give rise to this dharma-patience (dharmakṣānti).
The Buddha said:
"Devendra! The Buddha wishes to explain the life-span of the devaputra Candraprabha."
You should protect the true Dharma, receive it, uphold it, and practice it.
After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, during the final age when the Dharma is about to perish, you shall dwell here in Jambudvīpa.

In that world at that time, you shall bestow upon the people such profound and wondrous teachings as these—vast, immeasurable, and requiring diligent cultivation—and transform incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of people so that they abide in this Dharma-patience.

After the Dharma has completely vanished and his human life has ended, he will be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven in the presence of Maitreya Bodhisattva. There, he will receive and accept the subtle and wondrous teachings and transformations of these Buddhas, World-Honored Ones; he will establish immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devaputras in the state of non-arising, or cause them to resolve upon the path of unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.
"When Maitreya Bodhisattva attains perfect enlightenment, one shall dwell in Jambudvīpa for ten years making offerings.

Together with twenty thousand people, including Maitreya Tathāgata and his disciples, one shall leave home to enter the path, become a śramaṇa, receive and uphold the sūtras and the Dharma, and maintain the True Dharma throughout the remainder of one's life."

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, you shall use this Dharma to deliver all sentient beings; you will surely encounter all the thousand Buddhas who arise during this Bhadrakalpa, making offerings in succession to nine hundred and ninety-six World-Honored Buddhas.

They all cultivated the pure Brahma-faring under the Great Sage; after passing through seventy-five kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they soon attained the unsurpassed, right, and true path, becoming the Most Perfectly Enlightened Ones.
He shall be known as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Sūryaprabha, and his buddha-field shall be named Sarvaparipūrṇa.
Thereupon, the Devaputra Candrottara addressed the Prince Candra, saying:
“In this world, the World-Honored One has bestowed upon you the prediction that you shall attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path.”
"Why does the Tathāgata now rejoice in private with you alone, showing you particular compassion and bestowing upon you this prediction?
The Devaputra Candraprabha replied to Candrottarā:
"The Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, is forever free from desire; he has no difficulties and no knots of doubt."
Even if one were to receive a prediction of enlightenment without any expectation,
it is only because a bodhisattva has studied the conduct of a *kumārabhūta* that the Tathāgata grants them that prediction.
For what reason would the Tathāgata alone feel such joy, showing special compassion and pity to grant a prediction?
He asked again:
"O Son of Heaven!
With what kind of joyful faith should one seek within faith?"
He further said:

"If one conceives of the mind within the mind, that person is reckoned to have neither joy nor faith; they have nothing to grasp or take up, and for one who has nothing to grasp or take up, there is the foremost delight."
To reckon that within those [teachings] there is no flaw or impurity, and to have no sense of worldly joy—that is true faith and delight.
To find nothing to be said within words—that is true faith and delight.
He has never lacked joyful faith, nor does he harbor any resentment.
Therefore, O Devaputra,
if anyone seeks joyful faith, they should practice the Dharma that is beyond words.
The practice of diligent application is such that there is neither practicing nor non-practicing, and neither sorrow nor joy. Why is this?
Because the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) neither practices nor does not practice; it neither advances nor is indolent.
The Devaputra Candrottara addressed Candraprabha, saying:
"As for that which is called 'the training of a bodhisattva,' what does this mean?
Candraprabha replied:

"What is called the training of a bodhisattva is this: there is no body, nor does one guard the body; there is no tongue, nor does one guard the mouth; there is no mind, nor does one guard the mind—this is the foremost training of a bodhisattva."
That which is called "learning" is that which has nothing received and nothing practiced; if there is neither arising nor non-arising, this is the learning of a bodhisattva.
He asked again:
"Virtuous one!
Having studied this, has the Tathāgata bestowed a prediction of enlightenment upon you?"
He replied: "Devaputra!
It was not by studying this that I received the prediction of my enlightenment."
Why is this so? Because one who trains in this manner does not apprehend a self or what belongs to a self!
Not conceiving of or cognizing anything as being learned—this is called "training."
Neither in the heavens nor in the world can they find any deficiency in him, nor is there any loss.
If one should have the thought:
"I have something to learn," [then he is not a true disciple].
Thus, one does not proceed toward right action.
Failing to attain equanimity, one says of oneself:
"This is what I have studied."
Thus it is said. He asked again:
“By what means is it called ‘attaining equanimity’?”
He replied: "O Devaputra!
Suppose a practitioner neither ascends nor descends, does not abide in the middle, does not cling to what is practiced, and has nothing that is performed; [then he is liberated]."
