To practice while having nothing created is the bodhisattva’s practice.
One does not form the thought:
"This is a noble dharma; this is a base dharma."
"Regarding all these dharmas, one clearly understands their equality and does not give rise to dualistic thoughts.
A practitioner who acts in this way is said to have attained equality.
He asked again:
"What dharma has the worthy one now attained,
such that he has been granted a prediction of enlightenment by the Tathāgata?
Candraprabha replied:
“Nor did I eliminate the dharmas of ordinary beings, nor did I attain the dharmas of the Buddhas; it was by means of this that the Tathāgata bestowed upon me the prediction of enlightenment.
Within these dharmas, I have nothing to sever or eliminate, and regarding all dharmas, I have nothing to acquire; for this reason, I was granted the prediction.”
He asked again:
"If it were as you calculate, then all foolish and ignorant ordinary people would surely attain liberation. Why is this so?"
"Furthermore, one does not eliminate the dharmas of ordinary persons; this is precisely what is called being an 'ordinary person. How, then, could one bring about the Buddha-dharma?
He asked again:
"For what reason do you understand the dharmas of ordinary persons?"
The King of Moṅgolia replied:
"I understand the Buddha-dharma through the principle of emptiness as the realm of all phenomena.
As for that ultimate limit (pūrvakoṭi), it truly has no origin."
"Can the empty dharma-realm be extinguished?
He replied, "It cannot."
"The ultimate limit has no basis;
how could it be attained? He replied, "No."
"Therefore, O Son of Heaven!
It is for this reason that I say:
'I neither extinguish the dharmas of ordinary beings, nor do I attain the dharmas of the Buddhas; it is by means of this that the Tathāgata has bestowed upon me the prediction of enlightenment.'"
He asked again:
"Since emptiness and the fundamental limit of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) are without origin, are there any words [to describe them]?
He replied:
“There is none.
“If emptiness and the fundamental limit of the dharma-realm are fundamentally without origin, and there is no speech or path of verbal expression,
how can you now bestow a prediction of enlightenment upon this worthy one?”
He replied:
"O Son of Heaven!

The prediction now bestowed upon me is like the meaning of emptiness; the realm of all dharmas has no fundamental origin in its ultimate limit. This is the essential principle to which all dharmas return."

As phenomena are non-phenomena, so too is the reception of the prediction; as it is with the prediction, so too is the bestowal of individual enlightenment; as it is with the completion of the bestowal of individual enlightenment, so too is perfect awakening;
and even the attainment of the unsurpassed, right, and true path is likewise so.
Thereupon, the Devaputra Candrābha came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
The Devaputra Candrarāja has entered into profound wisdom that is lofty and difficult to equal."
The Buddha told the devaputra:

"When a bodhisattva has attained the patience of the dharma (dharmakṣānti), their dharma is such that they make distinctions; if they give rise to the principles of the Way and expound the sūtras, they liberate all matters within the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu)."
Furthermore, regarding that which is expounded as the dharma-realm, there are likewise no words to proclaim or demonstrate to the assembly. Why is this?
Because within the principle of the dharma-realm, there are neither words nor anything to be spoken.
Just as the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) is suchness, so too is the realm of sentient beings (sattvadhātu);
just as the realm of sentient beings is suchness, so too is the realm of the Buddha (buddhadhātu);
and the realm of the Buddha and the realm of phenomena are both suchness.
"If a bodhisattva enters into this meaning, they will be able to stand independently and not receive [teachings] from others.
*The Sutra on the Buddha Ascending to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Preach the Dharma for His Mother*, Middle Fascicle;
*The Sutra on the Buddha Ascending to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Preach the Dharma for His Mother*, Lower Fascicle.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty:

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana exhorted and inspired the assembly of countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of devaputras—the gods of the desire realm and the gods of the form realm—each of whom quickly took flowers, incense, powdered incense, blended incense, silken banners, and streamers. They each went to the Buddha to make offerings to the World-Honored One, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana returned to the Great Sage, prostrated himself on the ground, and withdrew to stand before the Buddha.
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana:

"Listen to the supernatural powers manifested by the Tathāgata and the transformations of the Perfectly Awakened One. There is a sutra titled 'The Tathāgata’s Manifestation of Majestic Transformations'; contemplate it well."
Maudgalyāyana replied,
“I shall listen as instructed.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:

"This trichiliocosm, consisting of ten billion suns and moons, ten billion great oceans, ten billion Sumeru kings of mountains, and ten billion sets of four continents—this is what is called a single Buddha-field within a trichiliocosm."
"What do you think?
Does the Buddha attain perfect enlightenment alone in a single Jambudvīpa?
Do not hold such a view."
Why is this? Because I have pervaded all the Buddha-worlds in the four directions, preaching the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings according to what is appropriate for them.
Some manifest the attainment of Buddhahood;
some further manifest themselves as being within the womb;
and some further manifest themselves in the Tuṣita Heaven.
"Or again, having manifested his body, he has entered parinirvāṇa.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"In this trichiliocosm, to the east, twelve thousand great four-continent worlds away from here, there is a world named Vimalā."
That Buddha is named Vimalamati Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently dwells preaching the Dharma.
In this world-system of four great continents belonging to that Buddha, the sentient beings have diminished lust, anger, and delusion, and are thus easily transformed and enlightened.
"There are few bodhisattvas training in the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas and many śrāvakas.
Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!

Whenever the Tathāgata Vimalamati assembles for each discourse on the Dharma, he guides nine hundred and ninety million śrāvakas; those transformed in that land do not distinguish between the four stages of realization as they do in this land, nor does he speak of the srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, or anāgāmin."
In that world, he sat for a single session to listen to the sutra, whereupon he realized the six supernormal powers and attained the eight stages of liberation.

Having acquired the power of spiritual travel, he leaped into the air to a height of four zhang and nine chi; fire issued from his body, which then consumed him in a self-immolation, after which he entered parinirvāṇa, suddenly vanishing into nothingness without smoke or embers.

In that land, the Tathāgata constantly preaches the Dharma without ever ceasing or desisting; he rescues and delivers all living beings without weariness, while the śrāvakas attain parinirvāṇa day after day.
Furthermore, they do not engage in trade, commerce, or the management of property; when they desire food and drink, these arrive according to their wishes without being conveyed by word of mouth.
Their clothing, food, dwellings, and houses are all for the sake of transforming beings, arising spontaneously like those in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, without passing through a womb.
The ground is made of purple gold.
The lifespan of the Tathāgata Vigatamala-mati is five hundred years, and the same is true for the people of that land; yet there are also those who die prematurely, Maudgalyāyana!
If you wish to know who that Tathāgata is who preaches the Dharma in that realm, could it be anyone else?
Do not harbor such a view. Why is this so?
This is precisely my own body!
As for the miraculous transformations and supernatural powers performed by the Buddha, they are beyond the reach of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:

"To the south of this trichiliocosm, eighteen great four-continent worlds away, there is a great four-continent world named Ratnavatī (Jewel-Formed), whose ground and trees are composed of the three treasures: gold, silver, and lapis lazuli."
There is a Buddha named Ratnagarbha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently dwells preaching the Dharma.

He exclusively expounds and proclaims the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas; those of the Śrāvaka vehicle are few, and those training as Bodhisattvas, as well as those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, are likewise rare.
If that land were suddenly to perish, one would be reborn in the empty buddha-realm of another direction and attain the path of a pratyekabuddha.
What do you think, Maudgalyāyana? Is this not so?
Regarding the Tathāgata who preached the *Ratnavigraha-parivarta Sūtra*, could he possibly be anyone else?
Do not harbor such a thought. Why is this so?
It is my very self.
When the Tathāgata manifests majestic spiritual transformations and expounds the Dharma therein, it is beyond the reach of knowledge for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"To the west of this trichiliocosm, twenty-two great four-continent worlds away, there is a realm of four continents named Ratnapaṭṭa."

The entire land was composed of the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, coral, amber, musaragalva, and agate; the trees throughout the realm were likewise transformed from various jewels, and the walkways, pavilions, railings, and gardens were all made of the seven treasures.
The bathing pools therein are filled with water of eight qualities, clear, limpid, and delicious;
just as the food, drink, and garments in the celestial palaces of the Tuṣita Heaven, so too are those of the people in that realm, being exactly equal without any distinction.
Furthermore, in that land there is not even the name "woman," nor are beings born from women.
The various classes of people do not give rise to impurity; they are born by transformation within lotus flowers, sitting in the full lotus posture.
The sentient beings in that land are free from lust, anger, and delusion; they have no thoughts of greed, no thoughts of malice, and no thoughts of harm, nor do they undergo birth from a womb.
That Buddha is named Ratnasaṃbhava Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently dwells preaching the Dharma.

What that Buddha teaches does not expound divergent meanings; he only expounds the treasury of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, the dhāraṇīs, the analysis of the three spheres, and the practice of the six pāramitās.
Those countless and inconceivable multitudes of sentient beings all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
Incalculable people attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
immeasurable people were granted the wisdom of the unsurpassed, right, and true path.

In that realm, even the names of the two vehicles do not exist; there is no speech or conduct of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. It consists purely of the Mahāyāna, is free from all sensual desires, and is entirely fresh, pure, and untainted, filled with a multitude of bodhisattvas.
The lifespan of that Buddha was eighty-four thousand years.
After their deaths, the people of the world did not go to the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, nor did they fall into the eight difficulties.
If these bodhisattvas should transfer their life-force, they will immediately be reborn in the presence of currently living Buddhas in pure Buddha-lands.

Devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, gandharvas, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas will all have a single resolve toward omniscience and the wisdom of the various supernormal powers; they will take no pleasure in divergent doctrines but will delight solely in the Buddha-dharma.
The physical forms, garments, movements, and gestures of devas, nāgas, and spirits cannot be distinguished from one another; they differ only in name.
Devas, nāgas, spirits, and the people of the world all share a single source and have no divergent streams.
What do you think, Maudgalyāyana?
Is the Tathāgata Ratnasaṃbhava anyone else?
It is he who, within that realm, expounds the Way of the Sūtras, awakening and transforming all the multitudes of beings.
Do not form such a view. Why is this?
Because it is my very self.
"This is the miraculous transformation of the Tathāgata’s supernormal power; it is not something that can be known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:

"To the north of this trichiliocosm, passing through thirty-six great four-continent systems, there is a four-continent realm named Fearless (Anuttrāsa), whose boundaries are formed of alternating gold and white silver."
In that land, there are no calamities of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, nor are there the terrors of the eight difficult states of existence.

The conduct of its people does not violate the precepts or involve false views; their dispositions are characterized by propriety and discipline, and none are violent or impetuous. Furthermore, even the names of non-Buddhist sects or heterodox schools are unknown there.
The Buddha’s name is Abhayamkara Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; he currently dwells there preaching the Dharma.
When that Buddha first went beneath the tree, seventy-two koṭis of Māras, including Sumati and others, approached, intending to do battle with the Buddha.
Furthermore, when that Tathāgata was a bodhisattva, practicing without negligence and accomplishing all supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), Māra attempted to obstruct his progress.
At that time, the Tathāgata manifested as many Buddha-trees as there were māras, and likewise transformed himself into as many bodhisattvas, each sitting separately beneath a Buddha-tree.
At that time, the various Māras were struck with unprecedented wonder, thinking:
"Who indeed is this that truly possesses the body of a bodhisattva?
We shall go there to obstruct and disrupt what he has undertaken, and destroy his resolve for the Way."
The emanated bodhisattvas said to the hosts of Māras:
"All dharmas are like illusions and transformations; what then do you, O virtuous ones, wish to disturb?
If you were able to discern and understand them, and thereby resolve to attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, that would be a source of merit and celebration."
If you further encourage others to resolve their minds on the Way,
yet obstruct those who have resolved their minds and come to corrupt and disturb them, you commit a grave offense;
you have never done so before, yet now you harbor such malice.
The various Māras asked again:
"What is the merit of one who resolves upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path, as well as one who exhorts and transforms others to resolve upon the Great Way?"
The Bodhisattva replied:

"Even if one were to fill as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges with the seven treasures and offer them in charity while aspiring for the Way, one's merit would surpass that."

Furthermore, even if all sentient beings throughout as many Buddha-lands as there are grains of sand in the Ganges were to collectively provide every kind of offering and serve all scholars, granting them whatever they desired;
"Furthermore, if there is someone who encourages another to resolve their mind on the Way, their virtue surpasses that of the former. He asked again:
"Suppose there is someone who disrupts or destroys the resolve for the Way; what would be the nature of their transgression?"
The bodhisattvas said:
"Suppose there were someone who were to go about plucking out the pupils of all sentient beings; would their transgression not be great?
They replied:
"Very much. He replied,
"The transgression of one who destroys the resolve for the Way is greater than that."
At that time, countless billions of hosts of Māras, hearing these words and witnessing this great transformation, all resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.
They offered celestial flowers, celestial incense, blended perfumes, scattered blossoms, and burning incense to the bodhisattvas, and played hundreds of thousands of varieties of musical instruments.
Each praised him in verse, saying:
"May the Noble Assembly swiftly attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.
At that time, when that Bodhisattva had attained supreme perfect enlightenment, a certain deva immediately raised his voice and said:
"Since all these hosts of Māras have been liberated from the evil realms and have resolved their minds upon the Way,
the Tathāgata has bestowed upon them the meaning of fearlessness.
For this reason, the Tathāgata is named 'One Who Possesses Fearlessness'."
Would you think that the Tathāgata Abhaya was anyone else?
Do not entertain such a view. Why is this?
"It is none other than my own body!
The Buddha said,
"Maudgalyāyana!..."

The Buddha transforms this name and manifests the preaching of the Dharma in that world; this is the miraculous response of the Tathāgata’s majestic spiritual power, which is beyond the reach of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:

"To the southeast of this trichiliocosm, eighty-four thousand *caturmahādvīpaka* world-systems away, there is a land named Universal Brocade Color. There, the Buddha is named Saṃkusumita Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently dwells and teaches the Dharma."
Those four great regions were variously and exquisitely adorned; their ground was composed of eight kinds of precious jewels and featured canopies of interlaced jeweled curtains.
The ground was as soft as the finest fine cloth, with precious grasses naturally growing four inches long, spread everywhere across it;
when one’s foot stepped upon them, they would sink down, and as soon as the foot was lifted, they would spring back to their original state.
Its ground was level and even, like the palm of a hand.

In the world of Universal Brocade there was a great city named Superior Sage, where the population was flourishing, peaceful, and free from calamity; rice and grain were cheap and abundant, happiness was beyond compare, and the people were numerous.
That city was one thousand two hundred and eighty li in length from east to west, and six hundred and forty li in width from south to north.
This great city of Uttara, where the people dwell, is so numerous as to be difficult to calculate; they are even more numerous than those in the kingdoms of Aṅga, Magadha, and Kaurava.

The Tathāgata Saṃkusumita constantly dwells in the great city of Uttarakuru. Whenever he preaches the Dharma once, he transforms three koṭis of people so that they attain the realization of arhatship;
three koṭis of people reach the stage of anāgāmin;
and three koṭis of people reach the tranquil practice of sakṛdāgāmin.
Three koṭis of people attained the realization of the stage of the path of seeing (srotāpatti-phala);
three koṭis of people were transformed into the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas;
and twice that number all gave rise to the aspiration for supreme, perfect, and true enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
There are countless people who have all planted the roots of manifold virtues.

Within the boundaries of those four great regions, there is a tree named "Honey-Composition," which is always in flower and fruit; its flavor is exceedingly delicious, like a banquet of a hundred flavors.

If a man or a woman takes these flowers and fruits and eats them, they will remain satiated for seven days and nights without hunger or thirst; their countenances will become beautiful and their complexions will transform; their vital essence will be full, their strength will be robust, and their bodies will be light and agile.
After consuming this food, they neither defecate nor urinate, nor do they have mucus or saliva.
They do not plow the soil, cultivate crops, or engage in trade to seek profit.
Clad in these flowers and fruits, they dwell naturally in peace and security.
There was neither poverty nor wealth; food, drink, dwellings, and so forth were without distinction.
Furthermore, the number of that Tathāgata’s śrāvakas was sixty-four billion, hundred thousand, nayutas, and the assembly of bodhisattvas was twice that number.
The pleasure garden where that Tathāgata wanders and contemplates is named Samantakusuma; it is the place where the Buddha takes his meals.
While the Buddha, together with the assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, was seated for the duration of a single meal, [the following occurred].
Immediately, all the trees bowed their branches in salutation, and these flowers and fruits naturally entered the bhikṣu’s bowl.
When the meal was finished, the various trees again bowed deeply and returned to their former positions as before.
The Buddha said,
“Maudgalyāyana!
The merit and glory of that world are as magnificent as this.”
The Tathāgata Saṃkusumita is none other than my own self.
He continues to exist in the present, preaching the meaning of the sutras under this very name; yet this is something that no śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas are able to know.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"To the southwest of this trichiliocosm, seven great four-continent worlds away, there is a realm in the four directions named Selection."
In each and every region there were eighty-four thousand kingdoms; in each kingdom there were eighty-four thousand kings; and each king had eighty-four thousand cities.

In that realm, with its great kingdoms, provinces, districts, counties, towns, villages, and hamlets, the population was fully complete, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of billions; all these kings abandoned what is contrary to the Dharma.
Each king had eighty-four thousand wives and court ladies; among all these court ladies, there was one who was the foremost in the land, a true jade maiden.
Each king had five hundred sons, or in some cases, one thousand two hundred sons.

Each of these kings governs the nation with righteousness; they do not employ whips or staves, nor do they set up blades of weapons. Each instructs and transforms their people so that they follow them spontaneously without being commanded.
There is a Buddha named Śrīratnaprabhāsa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently dwells there preaching the Dharma.
"In the monasteries throughout the four regions where that Buddha travels, the fragrant thrones are forty-nine feet high, and from each throne, a pervasive fragrance flows forth.

Heavenly flowers rain down upon the four continents, scattering over the Tathāgata Śrīratnaprabhāsa; hundreds of thousands of musical instruments resound spontaneously in harmony, and the heavens and earth suddenly shake with a great trembling, their sound like that of Brahmā. The accumulation of his merit is beyond measure."
The merit of hundreds of thousands is for the turning of the Wheel of Dharma; severing all worldly defilements and attaining the stainless Nirvana is called "protection.
The appearance of all Bodhisattvas listening to the Tathāgata preach the Dharma constitutes the four great elements.

The eighty-four thousand kings dwelling in the palace, along with their court ladies and all the men and women, great and small, having heard and understood the meaning of the Way, all attained the dharmas that are far removed from dust and free from defilement; the Dharma-eye arose within them.
The wives and children of all the kings, along with the members of their inner palaces, all resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment; with one voice, they each declared:
"We vow to leave the household life."
The Tathāgata exhorted and praised them, causing them all at once to become śramaṇas.

Whether they traveled through provinces, kingdoms, districts, towns, hamlets, or villages, even without planting or cultivating, non-glutinous rice grew spontaneously, and the devas all came to provide for them.

"At that Buddha’s first discourse on the Dharma, the assembly of śrāvakas all attained establishment in the fruit of srotāpanna, and those of the bodhisattva vehicle all attained the stage of adhimukti-kṣānti."

In the second preaching of the Dharma, they attained the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, and all those belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle fully attained the patient acceptance of the compliant Dharma (*anulomikī-dharmakṣānti*).
In the third assembly for the Dharma, as he expounded the sūtras, they dwelt in the state of *anāgāmin*, and the bodhisattva students attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).

In the fourth discourse on the Dharma, he established them in the state of Arhatship; the bodhisattvas who were training attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Among the kings, the women of the inner palace, and the official attendants, all transformed their female bodies and became men.
All these Tathāgatas have bestowed upon him the prediction that he shall all attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.
What do you think?
Is the Tathāgata in that realm named Śrīratnaprabha anyone other than this person?
Do not form such a view. Why is this?
It is none other than my own body!
By means of these names, he manifests and preaches the Dharma in those worlds.
Such transformations of the Tathāgata are beyond the capacity of any śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha to know.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"To the northwest of this trichiliocosm, at a distance of fifty-five great four-quadrant regions from here, there is a four-quadrant region named Gandhavatī."
With exquisite and superior sandalwood and various fragrant incenses as the soil of Jambudvīpa, there is a tree named Universal Fragrance (*Samantagandha*).

Each individual tree’s fragrance is sensed for forty *li*. Naturally produced lotuses, as large as chariot wheels, possess countless petals from which a pervasive fragrance flows; they are exceedingly soft and beautiful, like garments of the finest silk, with colors beyond reckoning and a brilliant radiance, growing to a height of twenty feet.
The fragrance of each individual lotus flower pervaded the four continents, its scent extending throughout immeasurable realms.
Fragrance formed multi-storied pavilions, and fragrance formed walkways;
from the ponds, lotus flowers sprang forth.
There were no commanderies, counties, kingdoms, cities, hamlets, or villages; there were only high towers numbering in the many thousands filling its borders.

It was like the sixth heaven, the Heaven of No-Strife (Nirmāṇarati), where the natural objects and the peace of the people, as well as their food, drink, recreation, and dwellings, were all equal without distinction.
When the Tathāgata of that land preaches the Dharma, he expounds only the pure teachings for great beings, setting aside the matters of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Bodhisattvas possessing supernormal powers pervade the four directions, and inconceivable multitudes of bodhisattvas have attained the patient acceptance of dharmas (dharmanidhyāna-kṣānti).

"Among the bodhisattvas, there was a bodhisattva named King Who Transforms All Dharmas. His aspirations were lofty and sublime; he had attained the three kinds of majestic accomplishment, and his patience, wisdom, supernormal powers, and eloquence were magnificent. He had made offerings to, prostrated before, and taken refuge in countless hundreds of thousands of millions of buddhas."
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Varṇavicitra-rāja-īśvara exhorted the World-Honored One to expound the sūtras, and the Buddha immediately granted his consent to proclaim the meaning of the Way.

Thereupon, rising from his seat before the Buddha to a height of four hundred li, he emitted rays of light from every pore that illuminated the entire world. Spontaneously, exquisite lotus flowers were manifested, each possessing countless hundreds of thousands of millions of petals; they spread throughout the realm, reaching a total height of four zhang and nine chi.
The musical instruments of the various devas played spontaneously without being struck, producing the sounds of the Dharma-seals of the eight classes of beings.

Each Dharma-seal encompassed the instructions of eighty-four billion scriptures, and each scripture contained twenty-two thousand eloquent words of fragrant incense, all of which were established naturally within the void.

Ninety-six hundred thousand billion people established themselves in non-retrogression, destined to attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, and all attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The assembly of bodhisattvas was thus pervasive throughout that land.

The people of that realm were free from blindness or deafness, nor were there any who were lame or crippled; they suffered neither from disfigurement, blemishes, or afflictions, nor was there anyone in want or poverty.

These bodhisattvas adorn their bodies with the thirty-two marks; they have no other pleasure than the Dharma as their joy, nor do they consume food or drink, but instead serve and honor [the Buddha] by being devoted to meditative concentration.
“They shall have no eight states of existence nor any evil destinies; even when their lives end, they shall have no other rebirth, but shall return solely to the Buddha-way.
The Buddha said, “Maudgalyāyana!”
"What do you think?
The Tathāgata Śubhaprabha was none other than my own self!
The transformations and manifestations performed by the Tathāgata therein cannot be known by any of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"To the northeast of this trichiliocosm, forty-two great four-sided regions away from here, there is a distinct great realm named Zhiwei."

The people of that land abound in lust, anger, and delusion; they are corrupt, evil, stingy, and greedy, clutching swords and staves in their hands. They lack faith, are envious, violate the precepts, and are full of malice. For the most part, they are fickle, indolent, arrogant, and impulsive; they let their minds run wild and act according to their whims, lacking any sense of composure or tranquility.

Conceiving of a self, they crave human life; furthermore, lacking wisdom, they do not know the proper seasons, nor do they understand shame or modesty; their disposition is impetuous and violent, and they are devoid of reverence.

The sentient beings in that land have countenances that are ugly, inferior, and lowly; they seek out each other's faults and desire to harm one another, delighting in mutual abuse, slander, and calumny.
The winds and rains do not come at their proper times, and perverse doctrines are taught to one another.
The ground is hard and rough with coarse defects; thorns and filth are spread throughout the land.

The people there have bodies and countenances resembling ice, sesame oil, or the blue color of plants; their clothing is ugly, their food and drink are coarse and poor, and they live in poverty and distress.
The seven types of calamities of earth and stone afflict the people, who harbor arrogant thoughts.
These celestial palaces belong to the people's faction; yet if they obtain wealth or treasures, it is all confiscated into the royal treasury.
The people of that land encounter various punishments and misfortunes, and when the pain of the staff is inflicted upon them, there is no distinction among any class.
The Buddha said,
“Maudgalyāyana!
Such are the sufferings and hardships currently experienced by the people of that land.”
Even if their lives were to end and they passed away, they would all fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
That Buddha’s name shall be Cittenakāruṇya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
He preached the Dharma and manifested the eighteen transformations while expounding the scriptures; yet during those seven hundred years, not a single person received his teachings.
That Buddha, the World-Honored One, did not grow weary or disheartened, but gave rise to great compassion and continued to expound the sutras with even greater diligence.

Whenever that Buddha enters a commandery, district, town, village, or hamlet, the people who see him all join together in reviling, slandering, insulting, and spitting upon him with contempt, and they strike him with tiles and stones.
Because that Honored Tathāgata desired to transform and guide them, he did not cease or rest.

At that time, the Buddha again preached the sutras for seven hundred years; eighty-four *koṭis* of people all attained the state of Arhat, while others attained the stages of Anāgāmin, Sakṛdāgāmin, and Srotāpanna—each group numbering eighty-four *koṭis*—and they all became śramaṇas on a single day, receiving the precepts of accomplishment.
At the conclusion of the three months, all those who were learners and those who were no longer learners ceased delighting in idle talk; within a single day, they all entered *parinirvāṇa*.

Furthermore, while that Tathāgata continued to remain in the world, there were again five persons who studied the Bodhisattva vehicle; having residual karmic stains from previous lives, they were born in that Buddha-land and encountered diligent suffering and affliction, whereupon the Buddha preached the sūtra for them.
Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying,
“By what transgressions or karmic retributions do the bodhisattvas of that land take birth in such a corrupt and evil place?
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"A bodhisattva gives rise to birth in evil realms and undergoes affliction and suffering through four matters.
What are these four?
If a bodhisattva craves offerings and profit, and does not study the Dharma of the Path, they will be born in an evil realm."
Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!
A bodhisattva also delights in slandering the true Dharma; not only does he fail to study it himself, but he also obstructs others, preventing them from receiving and upholding it.
Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!
When a bodhisattva rebukes or refutes others, they must not engage in slander by continuing to associate with them.
Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana,
a bodhisattva does not guard their body, speech, or mind.
"By means of these four dharmas, one is born into the evil realms and undergoes affliction and suffering.
The Buddha said,
"The one who expounded this sutra in that world was none other than myself."
“The Tathāgata’s manifestation of transformations and his awe-inspiring spiritual power are beyond the comprehension of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha:
“Does the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, perform the work of a Buddha only within this trichiliocosm, or does he also do so in other lands and different buddha-fields?”
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"What you have just seen is the World-Honored One manifesting himself together with the śrāvakas.

Furthermore, within this trichiliocosm of ten billion four-continent worlds, I likewise observe the inclinations and original aspirations of each person according to their preferences, preaching the Dharma to them individually."

Furthermore, within the four great regions of this trichiliocosm, the Buddha preaches the Dharma by manifesting the physical form and color of a Brahmā; or he appears in the likeness of a Tathāgata to teach and transform beings; or he manifests as a layperson not wearing the *kāṣāya* robe; or he appears like Śakra, teaching the Dharma; or like the Four Heavenly Kings or a Wheel-Turning Sage King. In all such ways, he employs skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) to preach the sūtras.

In this trichiliocosm, the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma to transform and enlighten each and every class of sentient beings who are to be delivered, according to what their respective minds delight in.
Furthermore, throughout immeasurable Buddha-lands in other directions, this is something that cannot be known by any of those of the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Like the palaces of the sun and moon, which do not move or shift, [the Tathāgata] appears everywhere in commanderies, kingdoms, counties, towns, villages, hamlets, districts, and great nations.

If the Tathāgata remains thus, unmoving within his own buddha-field, he nevertheless manifests in countless buddha-fields throughout all realms, preaching the sūtras in accordance with the fundamental inclinations and capacities of the various beings.
Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Regarding the Buddhas currently appearing, which one is the definitive reality:
the one in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven or the one in Jambudvīpa?"
"Are these the palaces of the various devas within the trichiliocosm?
Or are they those who preach the Dharma in other directions, in different Buddha-worlds?
O God among Gods, by what cause may one truly know and discern which is the authentic Buddha?"
"To which Buddha should one give so that the merit and blessings are vast and immeasurable?
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"I shall now question you; answer according to your own understanding."
"What do you think?
Suppose a magician conjures a person through his powers; is that person truly male or female?
Maudgalyāyana replied:
“There is no reality,
O God among Gods! Why is this so?
"Whatever is transformed through the power of illusory incantations is entirely non-existent and cannot be distinguished.
He asked again:
"Maudgalyāyana!"
"If one transforms according to what is appropriate, is there not something that can be explained?
He replied,
"I can explain it."
"The God among Gods!
The Buddha said:
"In this way, all dharmas are also like illusions and transformations; they cannot be distinguished, being equal and without distinction, and they do not act."
It is just as a magician, according to his power and incantations, performs many transformations; those who are transformed are all equal and without distinction.
The Buddha is also like this: by means of his holy wisdom, he universally manifests all Buddha-lands; what he creates is equal and without distinction, all constituting the work of a Buddha.
Those who make offerings to these Buddhas establish a measure of merit and blessings that is equal; there is no distinction among these Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
All these dharmas are entirely unarisen and lack substantial reality, being just like illusions and transformations.
"The dharmas are distinct, yet there is no differentiation between them.
The Buddha said,
"Maudgalyāyana!"

In the mere instant that the Tathāgata conceived this thought, he manifested from a single pore as many Tathāgatas, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River—each possessing the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, endowed with subtle and natural countenances—and transformed according to their forms to preach the Dharma universally, proclaiming it with sixty kinds of vocal tones.
All Tathāgatas clearly understand the mental activities of sentient beings and the inclinations of the masses; they know their roots and origins completely.
They preach the Dharma in accordance with the various beings, and whatever they expound is received by all sentient beings, whereby their suffering and afflictions are eliminated.

All these Tathāgatas, through three modes of manifestation and transformation, proclaim the various teachings of the Dharma; by means of the wisdom that discriminates with the four analytical knowledges, they fully manifest the virtues of a Buddha.
What do you think, Maudgalyāyana?
Which Tathāgata possesses the foremost and most supreme physical form and majestic appearance— was it the original one,
or was it the emanated Buddha?
"Is this a Tathāgata emanated by the Buddha?
Maudgalyāyana replied,
"There is no distinction between superior and inferior."
O God among Gods! Why is this so?
Because all transformations and changes are equal and without distinction; therefore, there is no difference.

"In their countenances, majestic presence, eloquence, and holy realization; in their supernormal powers, their preaching of the Dharma, and the beings they deliver—none can be distinguished as having any difference or distinction.
The Buddha said, "Therefore, Maudgalyāyana!"
"You should form this contemplation:
that which exists as a spontaneously manifested phenomenon has no distinction or peculiarity such that it cannot be differentiated.
The Buddha said:
“Maudgalyāyana!
If one thoroughly understands that all phenomena are naturally transformed, then one does not make distinctions by saying that ordinary persons are different;
how much less so for the Buddha-dharma! Why is this?
Maudgalyāyana!
All dharmas are fundamentally pure; all dharmas are empty.
Those who are deluded instead dwell upon manifold conceptualizations, judging what is appropriate and what is inappropriate, and they gallop about according to their own preferences.
That dharma-realm neither arises nor ceases.
The Tathāgata thoroughly understands the equality of the dharma-realm.

Those who understand this can, before all classes of sentient beings in Jambudvīpa, manifest the forms, marks, and signs of various Buddhas as well as various bhikṣus, yet cause the people to have no awareness of it.
"Set this aside, Maudgalyāyana!
Consider the people of Jambudvīpa;
even if one were to include all the gods, humans, and other beings born within the great realm of the four-sided Mount Sumeru, along with their various groups and assemblies."

The Tathāgata manifests entry into a single pore and displays transformations among the multitude of people, together with the assembly of noble ones; yet each individual among the people is unable to see one another, nor do they know where he has entered.
"Set this aside, Maudgalyāyana!
Suppose that all the classes of beings in the trichiliocosm were to gradually attain human form—every single living being, bhikṣus, noble assemblies, and the multitudes of people."
The Tathāgata manifests universally within a single pore, yet it is impossible to know what has entered there.
"Set this aside, Maudgalyāyana!

Suppose that all the Buddha-lands in the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, as well as the classes of sentient beings in the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, were to transform entirely and all attain human bodies."
The Tathāgata causes all people and the assembly of noble ones to enter into a single pore, yet he does not allow sentient beings to know that they have entered.
"Setting aside this, consider the multitudes of living beings in all the Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
The Buddha said, “Maudgalyāyana!

Now the Buddha, being present with unobstructed vision, beholds all buddha-fields. With the fully perfected, noble, penetrating Buddha-eye, one could employ various transformations as metaphors and speak of these buddha-fields for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, yet never reach their end.”
The buddha-fields are immeasurable and limitless.

Furthermore, if all these multitudes of sentient beings were to cause them all to attain the Way, such that they were like pratyekabuddhas, one could not calculate, measure, or know their limit; how much more so for śrāvakas!

Only the Tathāgata can know their quantity; he discerns all that exists within the lands—their breadth and narrowness, their size, their distance and proximity, their depth and shallowness—even down to a single hair, a fraction of an inch, or a divided atom.

Even if there were immeasurable, limitless, and incalculable numbers of worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, filled with dust particles, the Buddha’s infinite eye—through its unimpeded and holy penetration—sees them all.
These Buddha-lands surpass even those.

The multitudes of sentient beings within these Buddha-fields are immeasurable; such is the realm of humans that the number of living beings is exceedingly great, more numerous than the particles of earth.
These sentient beings gradually and successively attained human bodies;
all of them became universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), and for each of these monarchs, the number of their retinues was likewise as great as that of the original sentient beings.
All universal monarchs and their retinues, as well as the Tathāgata, are each able to enter into a single pore;
yet the holy assembly remains unaware of it, knowing not where they have entered.
Each saw, within every pore of the Tathāgata, the universal manifestation of Buddha-bodies and their assemblies of holy ones.
The majestic and miraculous transformations manifested by the Tathāgata never diminished or exhausted.

Even if one were to manifest transformations throughout a single kalpa, incalculable kalpas, or immeasurable and limitless kalpas, the light of the Tathāgata’s majestic, holy, and virtuous Way could never be fully described; such is his towering, divine, and wondrous nature.
"What do you think?
Is the merit obtained by the various wheel-turning kings and their seven treasures not great?
He replied:
"Very much, very much!
O God among Gods!
They abide immeasurably."
The Buddha said:
"Maudgalyāyana!
Now I tell you this."
If all classes of sentient beings were each to become a Wheel-Turning Sage King, and were to gather together all their blessings of the seven treasures,
this would not equal the merit produced by the Tathāgata for filling even a single pore.
"The auspiciousness resulting from virtuous merit transcends that [worldly realm] and cannot be compared to it.
At that time, the Venerable Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, so it is."
“World-Honored One!
I have attained excellent benefit through wisdom and other merits.
The Buddha, as the Dharma Master and Holy Honored One, possesses such infinite and wondrous spiritual power.”
His majestic power is infinite and his insight is clear and penetrating; vast and grand, his radiance is boundless and unfathomable.
Furthermore, the God among Gods, in all that he undertakes, suffers no diminution, for there is no dharma among all dharmas to which he does not attain complete mastery.

Because I have failed to manifest such a form and unimpeded wisdom, those sentient beings who hear of these sublime and majestic transformations performed by the Buddha—if they can with single-mindedness hear even a single phrase of its meaning—will obtain infinite benefit and boundless joy.

How much more so for those who believe in, uphold, recite, and read it; they shall immediately be endowed with such supernormal powers (ṛddhi-pāda) and give rise to the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
Such persons as these should take refuge in the God among Gods; they shall have no fear and need no longer doubt that they will fall into the evil destinies.

At that time, the devas, nāgas, spirits, Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings, having heard from the World-Honored One the manifestations, stirrings, and transformations displayed by the Buddha, praised him with one voice, saying:
“Homage to all Buddhas!”
I take refuge in the World-Honored One!
Should there be anyone who can give rise to such a mind with pure intent, I likewise take refuge in them and pay them homage;
they shall also cause the Great Way to flourish and shall surely attain its realization.
"If these transformations are indeed like those moved by the Tathāgata himself, we have no doubt and no lingering hesitation.

At that time, the devas, nāgas, spirits, gandharvas, Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings prostrated themselves on the ground with their five limbs to take refuge in this sutra. They then paid homage to the Buddha with reverent bows; hundreds of thousands of musical instruments resounded spontaneously, and they scattered celestial blue lotuses and stems of water lilies throughout the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

When the Buddha preached this sutra, seventy-two koṭis of devas and humans who had never previously resolved their minds toward the Way now all gave rise to the aspiration for supreme, true, and correct enlightenment.
Each of them spoke, saying:

"In a future age, before the devas and the people of the world, we shall proclaim and manifest the great lion’s roar, just as the Tathāgata has done today, giving rise to this guidance of the great lion’s roar."
Then the deva Candraprabha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If there are sons or daughters of good family who receive this sutra, uphold, recite, read, and extensively explain it to others, what merit and blessings will they obtain?”
The Buddha said:
"If sons or daughters of noble family receive this sutra, uphold, recite, read, and explain it to others, they shall encounter the Triple Gem without interruption."
Why is this? Those who hear this sutra do not give rise to the mind of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, but resolve solely upon the aspiration for the unsurpassed, right, and true path. Why is this?
Those who study this sutra will delight in its subtle and profound meaning; their faculties will be clear and penetrating, and they will possess faith and joy in all things.
Therefore, O Son of Heaven, you should form this view:
Those who are able to receive, uphold, recite, and read these sutras act to protect the Triple Gem so that it shall not be severed.
What do you think, O Son of Heaven? What is your assessment of this?
"As for those who protect the Three Jewels so that they are never severed— even if a thousand Buddhas were each to live for an entire kalpa, could they ever exhaustively praise their merit?
He replied, "They could not."
"The God among Gods!
The Buddha said,
"For this reason, Son of Heaven, you should understand that if there are those who receive and uphold this sutra, their merit shall be immeasurable."
Thereupon, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is the name of this sutra?
By what cause should it be upheld by its name?"
The Buddha told Maitreya:
"This sutra is titled 'The Chapter on the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven: The Buddha’s Manifestation of Awe-Inspiring Miracles'; uphold it."
The Buddha said, "Maitreya!
Those who zealously receive, uphold, recite, and explain this, and who analyze and clarify its meaning for others, will achieve much."
"For the multitude of people, it is extremely difficult to encounter such a sūtra as this being circulated throughout the world.
Thus spoke the Buddha.

The Devaputra Candraprabha, the Devaputra Candrābha, the Bodhisattva Maitreya, the Venerable Maudgalyāyana, and all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and the people of the world were filled with joy; they paid homage and withdrew.
